transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-06
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Mia Torres (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Rao (EdenPath Head of Platform), Sam Nguyen (EdenPath SRE), Jordan Lee (Product)
Link to deck: https://redwood.example.com/decks/edenpath-diagnostics (note: placeholder)

Summary: Hands-on console walkthrough focused on live request tracing, error analysis, and replay/bench capabilities. Customer wants replication of a production failure pattern and guidance on private vs hosted tradeoffs.
Topics: runtime tracing, request logs, KV cache behavior, prefix caching, request replay/bench, SOC2/KMS, SSO, pilot timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick audio check?
[00:04] Dr. Priya Rao: audio is good, thanks. we've been looking forward to this, we had a couple of incidents last quarter with tokenization blowups so wanting to see your request playbook.
[00:15] Alex: awesome, yeah we'll jump into the console. i'm alex, i'm the AE working with edenpath, and mia will walk through the runtime diagnostics sandbox.
[00:25] Mia: hi all, quick intro from me — i own the diagnostic tooling and the bench configs. i'll be doing the live part — heads up the transcript might have some small ASR weirdness, so i'll call out key logs.
[00:34] Sam: cheers. our main constraints are: 1) we need private deployment or VPC peering because of PHI, 2) 99th percentile latency matters for real-time triage, and 3) we want strong auditability.
[00:46] Alex: noted. and timeline? you mentioned a pilot in october in the email, is that still the plan?
[00:51] Jordan: yes, product would like a two-week pilot then move to a month-long POC if bench results look good.
[00:57] Mia: ok, we'll aim for bench in the next week. i'll show the trace map, request inspector, and a replay bench that runs on your prompt set.

[01:12] Mia: opening the console — top left you can see the live stream of requests, there's the request id, model variant, routing tier. notice the little flame icon, that's our cost/latency tag. sometimes ASR will show it as 'plan' so don't worry.
[01:30] Mia: here's an example request that hit a fallback — you'll see the stepdown from the dedicated pool to the hosted variant, and a trace showing the KV cache miss sequence.
[01:40] Dr. Priya Rao: can you expand the trace? i want to see where the tokenization error appears.
[01:44] Mia: sure — so the trace timeline shows: tokenization -> prefix cache lookup -> model inference -> post-processing. at 00:00:12 we have a tokenization exception then an automated retry path that changed batch size from 8 to 1 which explains the latency spike.
[02:05] Sam: that batching change — is that the runtime auto-tuner? or something in our client?
[02:09] Mia: that's our runtime policy — continuous batching tries to maximize throughput but on certain malformed tokens the model returns a decode error and our fallback flow will reduce the batch to single-request mode and route to a compatible quantized variant.
[02:26] Alex: that's a great thing to test in the bench — show the percentiles before and after.

[02:40] Mia: toggling the request details panel — here you can see request headers (client id obfuscated), the prompt snippet, and the KV cache key hits. note the key naming mismatch: edenpath-prod -> edenpath_production, sometimes hyphen vs underscore causes misses — small ops detail but big perf hit.
[02:58] Jordan: ugh, we do have inconsistent naming in our migration, that could be the root cause.

[03:05] Mia: switching to the error-analysis tab — this aggregates errors by model variant and by route. the console auto-links to the raw log lines and the exact stack trace captured by our request inspector.
[03:20] Mia: here's a sample stack — ASR transcribed 'K V cahce' instead of KV cache, you'll see 'kvCache.get' then a null pointer leading to a fallback, that null was from an upstream client not populating a session id.
[03:34] Sam: we'd like to enforce session id at ingress — is there an easy way to block those at the routing layer?
[03:38] Mia: yes, you can add a routing pre-check rule in the console — i've got a snippet i'll share. it returns a 400 and logs the incoming headers if session-id missing, preventing the fallback churn.

[03:52] Alex: question from the procurement/security side — what does audit logging look like in private deployments?
[03:57] Mia: in private we ship a control-plane agent that pushes audit events to your S3/GCS bucket or your SIEM via Kinesis. events are signed and you can route them to your on-prem HSM for key management. we also support customer-managed KMS keys for model encryption at rest.
[04:15] Dr. Priya Rao: SOC2? do you have certs and a penetration report?
[04:19] Alex: yes, we have SOC2 and ISO artifacts — i'll send the package. we also have SOC2 attestation for the private control plane; the on-prem package can run air-gapped if needed.
[04:30] Jordan: what about SSO? we use SAML 2.0.
[04:33] Mia: SAML is supported for console auth; for API keys we recommend rotating keys and using short-lived tokens tied to your IdP. we can also integrate with your SCIM group mappings for RBAC.

[04:48] Mia: back to the replay bench — i'm going to simulate a 1k concurrent user burst with your anonymized prompts. watch the request map — you can see a cluster of retries at t+00:02 when the load exceeds the dedicated pool threshold.
[05:03] Mia: the console shows latency heatmap and token-cost projection. note that enabling prefix caching reduces token re-gen by ~30% on repeated prompts, but also increases memory usage on the worker.
[05:18] Sam: memory is fine for us, but we need predictable p95 < 200ms for the triage UI. can you guarantee that on dedicated?
[05:25] Mia: dedicated gives you predictable throughput; our SLA is on the availability and a model-tier latency target — p95 guarantees are configurable depending on pool size. i'll include recommended pool sizing in the bench report.

[05:40] Mia: switching to the request-inspector replay — selecting a failed transaction and clicking 'replay sandbox' brings up a side-by-side diff: original output vs replay. here the replay on quantized-4bit yields slightly different punctuation and a longer tail token, that's expected with different quantization and you can add an eval to measure regression.
[06:02] Dr. Priya Rao: when you say regression, how do we track regressions? we need a gating policy before rollouts.
[06:08] Alex: Redwood Optimize has eval sets and automated regression alerts — you can tie an eval to a rollout and fail the canary if MRR drops or hallucination count increases.
[06:18] Jordan: will that work for our templates? our prompts have a strict schema.
[06:22] Mia: yes, we can attach structural validators and function-calling checks so you get errors if the JSON shape differs.

[06:32] Sam: quick nit — you mentioned KV cache key mismatch earlier. is there a way to view key usage over time?
[06:38] Mia: yes there's a KV-usage graph by prefix. it shows hit/miss, and you can set alerts on miss-rate. note: ASR sometimes transcribed that graph as 'queen vee usage' which is amusing.

[06:50] Mia: now i'll show an incident drill — we've got a synthetic trace that simulates an upstream tokenization service returning a non-utf8 sequence. starting trace.
[07:00] [07:00] Mia: trace shows tokenizer exception at 00:00:03, fallback to hosted variant at 00:00:06, auto-retry at 00:00:10. the trace inspector correlates to the log lines and to a snapshot of the payload.
[07:20] Alex: if we wanted to prevent the fallback and instead fail-fast, is that configurable?
[07:25] Mia: yep route policies include 'fail-fast', 'retry-with-strict-preprocessing', or 'route-to-dedicated-only'. you can set it per-route or per-customer.

[07:35] Jordan: any impact on cost if we set fail-fast versus retries?
[07:38] Mia: fail-fast reduces cost because fewer retries, but could increase error surface for end-users. retries increase token usage and adds compute. there's a simple tradeoff graph in the console cost tab.

[07:50] Dr. Priya Rao: on data residency — we need to ensure inference logs with PHI don't leave our VPC. can the private control plane keep logs on-prem?
[07:58] Mia: yes you can configure the control-plane agent to persist logs to your S3 or to push to an on-prem ELK. we also offer a deployment where the control plane sits inside your VPC and nothing traverses public endpoints.

[08:12] Sam: what's the onboarding friction for our infra team? we run k8s with our own node pool.
[08:18] Mia: we provide a helm chart for private deploy, and an on-prem bundle for air-gapped installs — typical install takes 2-3 days for an initial dev cluster, full production on-boarding 2-4 weeks. we also have a managed dedicated option if you want Redwood-managed infra in a dedicated VPC.

[08:40] Mia: ok switching to live bench results — here's the latency CDF for your sample. see the grey ramp is baseline, the orange is with prefix cache enabled, and the blue is the fallback-path experiment.
[08:55] Sam: i see a tail at 98th percentile around 420ms in the blue — what drives that?
[08:59] Mia: that's the fallback routing and the quantized variant decode penalty. if we add cross-model warm caches (we keep KV cache warm across variants) that tail drops to ~190ms in our tests.
[09:15] Jordan: warm caches across variants — does that have consistency implications?
[09:18] Mia: only if you mix model families with different tokenization. same family with different quantization is fine; mixing families you need a token mapping.

[09:28] Alex: i want to surface a common question — how does continuous batching interact with low-latency SLOs?
[09:34] Mia: continuous batching tries to batch within your latency window; for strict p95 SLOs you set a latency cap and the runtime will flush partial batches. the console exposes a live metric 'batch wait time' so ops can tune it.

[09:50] Mia: showing request log raw view — note we keep a compressed token-level trace for 7 days by default, extendable. logs show model inputs with sensitive parts redacted if you enable PIIR filters.
[10:05] Dr. Priya Rao: redaction — can we control what is redacted? our PHI markers are custom.
[10:09] Mia: yes, custom redaction rules supported — regex and structured field masking. they run pre-ingest so nothing sensitive persists unless you allow it.

[10:22] Sam: quick question on cost modeling — our finance lead wants a prediction for 100k monthly queries with average 120 tokens.
[10:30] Alex: we have an exportable cost model from Optimize; i'll attach a sample sheet. in short, prefix caching and batching reduce per-token cost significantly, and quantization reduces GPU memory and instance cost.

[10:44] Mia: wrapping the interactive part — i've dropped a couple links in chat: bench config template, the routing-policy snippets, and the pre-ingest redaction docs.

[10:55] Jordan: about pilot acceptance criteria — product wants 95% of core flows to have identical structured outputs, less than 1% hallucination increase, and p95 < 200ms. is that realistic?
[11:07] Mia: realistic with tuned pool sizing and warm KV cache, yes. we'll quantify in the bench report.

[11:16] Alex: ok let's recap next steps so everyone's aligned.
[11:20] Alex: action items — mia will run the 2-hour bench, alex will send security pack, sam will provide test prompts and SSO metadata.
[11:29] Dr. Priya Rao: sounds good. also can we get a short doc describing the failover behavior between hosted and dedicated variants?
[11:33] Mia: yes we'll include a playbook and the routing-policy snippets.

[11:40] Alex: any final questions?
[11:42] Sam: one more — do you support hardware token signatures on audit logs? we use a YubiHSM cluster.
[11:49] Mia: we can sign events with customer KMS; integrating with YubiHSM via PKCS#11 is supported in the private control plane. i'll note that in the security pack.

[11:59] Alex: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the bench run.
[12:04] Dr. Priya Rao: thanks, looking forward to it.

[12:10] End of recording

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels are human-assigned but ASR occasionally mis-tokens technical terms (e.g., 'K V cache' transcribed differently); pauses and cross-talk retained.
